agent_facts.chief_complaint: Runny nose and mild sore throat for 2 days

evidence: No fever
I'm still eating and drinking fine

agent_judgment.rationale: Two days of rhinorrhea and mild sore throat without fever, with normal eating and drinking, fits an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection. There are no red flags such as breathing difficulty, drooling, inability to swallow, high fever, or dehydration. Home care with clear return precautions is appropriate. No question is likely to change the disposition, since red-flag symptoms are covered by the safety net.
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Escalate if the patient reports any of the following: difficulty breathing or shortness of breath; inability to swallow saliva, drooling, or a muffled 'hot potato' voice; severe one-sided throat pain or neck swelling; trouble opening the mouth; signs of dehydration; fever of 39°C (102.2°F) or higher; symptoms worsening after initial improvement; or symptoms lasting beyond 10 days. Also escalate if the patient is immunocompromised or turns out to be an infant.
agent_judgment.safety_net: Seek care right away (urgent care, ER, or 911) for difficulty breathing, inability to swallow your own saliva or drooling, a muffled voice, severe one-sided throat pain or neck swelling, trouble opening your mouth, or confusion. Message us for a visit if you develop a fever above 39°C (102.2°F), a sore throat that becomes severe without cough, symptoms that get better and then worse, symptoms lasting more than 10 days, ear pain, or facial or sinus pain with fever.
agent_judgment.patient_reply:
Thanks for reaching out. A runny nose and mild sore throat for a couple of days, with no fever and normal eating and drinking, sounds like a common cold, which is a viral infection. It usually improves on its own within 7–10 days. Antibiotics don't help colds.

Things that can help:
- Rest and plenty of fluids.
- Warm drinks, honey (not for children under 1), throat lozenges, or salt-water gargles for the throat.
- Saline nasal spray or rinses for congestion.
- Acetaminophen or ibuprofen for discomfort, if these are safe for you. Follow the package directions.
- Wash your hands often to avoid spreading it.

Please get care right away (urgent care, ER, or call 911) if you have:
- Trouble breathing.
- Can't swallow your own saliva, or are drooling.
- A muffled voice.
- Severe pain on one side of your throat, neck swelling, or trouble opening your mouth.

Send us a message so we can arrange a visit if:
- You develop a fever above 39°C (102.2°F).
- Your sore throat becomes severe.
- You start feeling better and then get worse.
- Symptoms last more than 10 days.
- You develop ear pain or facial pain with fever.

I hope you feel better soon!

baseline.rationale: Two days of runny nose and mild sore throat without fever, with normal eating and drinking, fits a common viral upper respiratory infection (cold). No red flags are reported. Home care is appropriate, with return precautions for signs of strep, bacterial sinusitis, airway compromise or lower respiratory involvement.
baseline.escalation_trigger: Escalate to WITHIN_48H for any of these: fever 38.3°C (101°F) or higher with a severe sore throat and no cough, white patches on the tonsils, or tender swollen neck glands (possible strep); symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement; or worsening after initial improvement. Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW for any of these: trouble breathing, inability to swallow saliva or drooling, muffled voice, a stiff neck, inability to open the mouth fully, or signs of dehydration.
baseline.safety_net: Seek care urgently if you develop trouble breathing, can't swallow your own saliva, have a muffled voice, a stiff neck, or can't open your mouth fully. Message us if you develop a high fever, white patches on your tonsils, or swollen tender neck glands. Also message us if symptoms last beyond 10 days, or if they improve and then get worse again.
baseline.patient_reply:
Hi, thanks for reaching out. What you're describing sounds like a common cold, which is caused by a virus. It's not something to be worried about. Colds usually peak around days 2–3 and improve over 7–10 days, though a mild cough can linger a bit longer. Antibiotics won't help a viral cold.

Things that can help you feel better:
- Rest and plenty of fluids.
- Warm drinks with honey, throat lozenges, or salt-water gargles for the sore throat.
- Saline nasal spray or rinses for the runny nose.
- Acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label if your throat hurts. Skip ibuprofen if you have kidney problems, stomach ulcers, or have been told to avoid it.
- Wash your hands often to avoid spreading it to others.

Please message us if you notice any of these:
- A fever of 101°F (38.3°C) or higher, especially with a very sore throat, white patches on your tonsils, or swollen tender glands in your neck.
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days.
- You start to get better and then get worse again.

Get care right away (urgent care, ER, or 911) if you have any of these:
- Trouble breathing.
- Can't swallow your own saliva, or you're drooling.
- A muffled voice or a stiff neck.
- Can't open your mouth fully.
- Signs of dehydration, like very little urine or feeling dizzy when you stand.

Feel better soon!

If you have nitroglycerin that was prescribed for you, follow its instructions, but do not take someone else's. This fits uncomplicated acute cystitis, which a physician can typically treat asynchronously with empiric antibiotics without an in-person visit. No features suggest pyelonephritis or a complicated infection. Vaginal symptoms or STI risk would point toward vaginitis or cervicitis, which needs in-person testing. Systemic symptoms or upper-tract signs would require same-day evaluation.
clarifying_questions: Do you have any new vaginal discharge, itching, or irritation, or a new sexual partner in the past few months?
Do you have nausea, vomiting, chills, or shaking?
Do you have diabetes, a weakened immune system, kidney problems, or any known urinary tract abnormality? Have you had a UTI or antibiotics in the past 3 months?
Do you have any medication allergies, especially to antibiotics?
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW (urgent care or ED today) for any of the following: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, flank or back pain, nausea or vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down. Escalate to WITHIN_48H for in-person testing for vaginal discharge or itching or a new sexual partner. A history of diabetes, immunocompromise, urologic abnormality, or a recent UTI or antibiotic course makes this a complicated infection and calls for a urine culture. If she does not reply, the disposition stays ASYNC_PHYSICIAN: the physician can still treat as uncomplicated cystitis based on the facts given.
agent_judgment.safety_net: Go to urgent care or the emergency department today if you develop fever, chills, pain in your back or side, or nausea or vomiting, or if you start to feel very unwell. Contact us if your symptoms are not clearly improving within 48 hours of starting treatment, if they come back after treatment, or if you notice vaginal discharge.

agent_facts.chief_complaint: Red, swollen cut on bottom of foot

evidence: I'm diabetic
No fever.
I got a small cut on the bottom of my foot about 4 days ago and now the skin around it is red and a little swollen
It's tender when I press on it.

agent_judgment.rationale: A diabetic foot wound with new redness, swelling and tenderness 4 days after injury is a likely early diabetic foot infection. She needs an in-person exam (wound assessment, probe-to-bone, possibly X-ray and labs) and probably antibiotics within 24-48 hours. Diabetic foot infections can progress quickly and threaten the limb, and diabetes can blunt fever and pain, so the absence of fever is not reassuring. Signs of moderate or severe infection (spreading redness more than 2 cm from the wound, streaking, pus or foul odor, dark or dead tissue, crepitus, systemic symptoms, or uncontrolled glucose) would make this an emergency today. The questions below screen for those signs.
clarifying_questions: How far does the redness extend from the edge of the cut? More or less than about 2 cm (roughly 1 inch)? Is it spreading, or are there red streaks going up your foot or leg?
Is there any pus, drainage or bad smell, or any skin around the cut that looks dark, black, blistered or crackly?
Do you have chills or shaking, or feel generally unwell? Are your blood sugars running much higher than usual?
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW if any of the following apply: redness extends more than 2 cm from the wound or is spreading, red streaks, pus or foul odor, dark/black or blistering skin, crackling under the skin, chills, feeling unwell, fever, vomiting, or blood sugars much higher than usual or hard to control. No reply does not lower urgency. She still needs an in-person exam within 24-48 hours.
agent_judgment.safety_net: Go to the emergency department today if the redness spreads or streaks, the pain or swelling gets quickly worse, pus or a bad smell appears, the skin turns dark or blistered, or you develop fever, chills or high blood sugars. Until you're seen: keep weight off the foot, keep the cut clean and covered, check your sugars more often, and check the foot daily, since numbness can hide worsening.
agent_judgment.patient_reply:
Thank you for letting us know. Because you have diabetes, a cut on the foot that becomes red, swollen and tender needs prompt attention. This may be an early infection, and foot infections in people with diabetes can worsen quickly even without a fever. You need to be seen in person within the next 24-48 hours, ideally within 24 hours, so the wound can be examined. You may need an X-ray, blood tests or antibiotics. Please book a visit with us or go to urgent care if we can't see you in time.

To help us, please reply with:
1. How far does the redness extend from the edge of the cut (more or less than about 1 inch)? Is it spreading, or are there red streaks up your foot or leg?
2. Is there any pus, drainage or bad smell, or any skin that looks dark, black or blistered?
3. Do you have chills or feel generally unwell? Are your blood sugars higher than usual?

If you answer yes to any of these, please go to the emergency department today instead of waiting.

Until you're seen: keep weight off that foot as much as possible, gently clean the cut with soap and water, cover it with a clean dry dressing, check your blood sugar more often, and look at the foot at least once a day. Go to the emergency department right away if the redness spreads, the pain or swelling quickly gets worse, pus or a bad smell appears, the skin darkens, or you develop a fever, chills or very high blood sugars.

baseline.rationale: A 62-year-old with diabetes has a 4-day-old plantar foot wound with localized redness, swelling and tenderness, consistent with an early (likely mild) diabetic foot infection. She has no fever. Diabetic foot infections can progress quickly and are often under-signaled because of neuropathy and impaired immune response. She needs an in-person exam within 24-48 hours to assess wound depth, extent of redness, probe-to-bone and pulses, and likely to start oral antibiotics, with imaging if the wound is deep. Features of moderate or severe infection would move this to same-day emergency care: redness extending more than 2 cm from the wound, lymphangitic streaking, purulence, necrosis or black tissue, crepitus, a deep wound, systemic symptoms, or markedly elevated glucose.
clarifying_questions: How far does the redness spread from the edge of the cut? Is it more than about 2 cm (roughly the width of your thumb), and is it getting bigger?
Do you see any red streaks running up your foot or leg, or any pus, cloudy drainage, or a bad smell from the cut?
Is any of the skin around the cut turning dark, black, or blistered, or does the cut look deep?
Have your blood sugars been running higher than usual (for example, consistently over 300), or do you feel unwell, with chills, nausea, or confusion?
Do you have numbness in your feet or known circulation problems in your legs?
baseline.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW if: redness extends more than 2 cm from the wound or is spreading, red streaks appear, there is pus, foul odor, or dark or black skin, the wound is deep, fever or chills develop, blood sugars are markedly elevated (over 300) or she feels systemically unwell, or the pain is worsening rapidly. If there is no reply, the staff should still book an in-person visit within 24-48 hours and attempt outreach, since current findings alone warrant an exam.
baseline.safety_net: Go to urgent care or the emergency department today if the redness spreads, red streaks appear, pus or a bad smell develops, the skin turns dark, you get a fever or chills, your sugars run very high, or you feel unwell. Diabetic foot infections can worsen quickly.
baseline.patient_reply:
Thank you for letting us know. Because you have diabetes, redness, swelling and tenderness around a foot cut can be an early infection. Diabetic foot infections can get worse quickly, so I'd like you to be seen in person within the next 24-48 hours, ideally sooner. You may need antibiotics, and we'll check how deep the wound is and how the circulation in your foot is.

Until then:
- Gently wash the cut once or twice a day with mild soap and water, pat it dry, and cover it with a clean, dry bandage. Don't soak your foot.
- Stay off the foot as much as you can and avoid walking barefoot.
- Draw a line with a pen around the edge of the redness so you can tell if it's spreading.
- Check your blood sugar more often than usual.

To help me decide how soon you need to be seen, please reply with:
1. How far does the redness spread from the cut? More than about 2 cm (a thumb's width)? Is it growing?
2. Any red streaks going up your foot or leg, or any pus, cloudy drainage, or bad smell?
3. Is any skin around the cut dark, black, or blistered, or does the cut look deep?
4. Have your sugars been higher than usual (for example, over 300), or do you feel unwell?
5. Do you have numbness in your feet or known circulation problems?

Please go to urgent care or the emergency department today, without waiting for a reply, if the redness spreads past your pen line, red streaks appear, pus or a bad smell develops, the skin turns dark, you get a fever or chills, your sugars are very high, or you feel unwell. Our team will reach out to schedule your visit.

agent_facts.chief_complaint: Hopelessness and thoughts others better off without them

evidence: Last night I caught myself thinking everyone would be better off without me.
I've been feeling really hopeless for a few weeks now.

agent_judgment.rationale: Passive suicidal ideation (thinking others would be better off without them) after several weeks of hopelessness suggests a depressive episode with suicide risk. Passive ideation without a reported plan or intent does not by itself require emergency care, but it does require immediate human outreach and an in-person or live mental health assessment within 48 hours at the latest. The answers to the questions below could make this an emergency, so 48 hours is the minimum, not the default. The patient's distress ('I don't know what to do') increases concern.
clarifying_questions: Are you having any thoughts of ending your life or hurting yourself right now?
Have you thought about how you might do it, or made any plans or preparations?
Do you have access to anything you could use to hurt yourself, such as firearms, stockpiled medications, or other means?
Have you ever tried to hurt yourself or end your life in the past?
Are you using alcohol or drugs more than usual, and is there someone with you or nearby whom you trust?
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW (911, 988, or the emergency department) if the patient reports current intent, any plan or preparation, access to lethal means they are thinking of using, a recent attempt, intoxication, or feeling unable to stay safe. Also escalate if the patient does not respond to outreach promptly. A crisis-trained human should attempt live contact today regardless.
agent_judgment.safety_net: If thoughts of ending your life become stronger, you start thinking about how you would do it, or you feel you can't keep yourself safe, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or call 911, or go to the nearest emergency department right away. Do not wait for a reply from us. If possible, stay with someone you trust and move firearms or extra medications out of reach.
agent_judgment.patient_reply:
Thank you for telling us. It took courage to write this, and I'm really glad you reached out. Feeling hopeless for weeks and having thoughts that everyone would be better off without you is serious, and you deserve support with it. You don't have to figure this out alone. A member of our care team will try to contact you directly today. You can also call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) at any time, day or night, to talk with someone right now.

To help us support you, please answer these as soon as you can:
1. Are you having any thoughts of ending your life or hurting yourself right now?
2. Have you thought about how you might do it, or made any plans?
3. Do you have access to firearms, a supply of medications, or anything else you could use to hurt yourself?
4. Have you ever tried to hurt yourself before?

We want to see you for an assessment within the next 1–2 days to talk about how you're feeling and about treatment options that can help, such as therapy and medication.

Please don't wait for our reply if things get worse. Call 911 or 988, or go to the nearest emergency department right away if any of these happen:
- the thoughts get stronger
- you start planning how you would do it
- you feel you can't keep yourself safe

If you can, reach out to someone you trust to be with you, and put firearms or extra medications somewhere out of reach. Depression is treatable, and things can get better.
